_README: Approach variants — Washington Snoqualmie Pass / Alpine Lakes, 2026-08-19. 39 routes, 42 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name. Five of these ids carry
no peak name at all — wa_south_face_7 and wa_east_ridge_7 are RED MOUNTAIN (Snoqualmie), wa_east_ridge_6 is MOUNT THOMSON,
wa_southwest_face and wa_east_face_variation are THE TOOTH, wa_south_gully_south_spur and wa_blood_sport are GUYE PEAK, and
wa_new_york_gully is SNOQUALMIE MOUNTAIN. A name-shaped id is not evidence of which peak you are on.
Scope was the 24 named peaks plus Huckleberry Mountain, which sits in the same PCT corridor between Alaska Mountain and
Chikamin and is reached by the same walk. Areas queried: wa_alta_mountain, wa_bears_breast_mountain, wa_big_snow_mountain,
wa_bryant_peak, wa_cathedral_rock, wa_chair_peak, wa_chikamin_peak, wa_chimney_rock, wa_denny_mountain, wa_guye_peak,
wa_hibox_mountain, wa_huckleberry_mountain, wa_kaleetan_peak, wa_kendall_peak, wa_lemah_mountain, wa_lemah_two,
wa_mount_daniel, wa_mount_hinman, wa_mount_thomson, wa_overcoat_peak, wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie, wa_snoqualmie_mountain,
wa_summit_chief_mountain, wa_the_tooth, wa_three_queens. 68 routes live in them; 17 already carried approach_variants and
were not touched. Of the 51 with an EMPTY approach_variants, 39 are written here and 12 were deliberately skipped — see _SKIPPED.
Contamination rejected during research, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- wa_chimney_rock_west_face is an IDAHO route (Selkirk Crest) filed on Washington's Chimney Rock and already flagged for
removal. It was NOT enriched. Washington's Chimney Rock carries only East Face and East Face Direct, and both already
have approach_variants.
- 'East Ridge' on Red Mountain names THREE different things: the short bolted pitch above Red Pass that this DB row
describes, a SummitPost page describing the whole saddle-to-summit traverse over two false summits, and a second
SummitPost page describing a ridge traverse from Point 5720 near the Kendall Katwalk whose own author advises against
repeating it. Each was matched by pitch count and by the ground it covers, not by name.
- Mount Thomson is spelled Thompson on roughly half the published sources, and 'West Ridge' is a SummitPost page title
shared with several unrelated peaks. Matched by the Bumblebee Pass approach and the 1940 Beckey first ascent.
- 'Northeast Buttress' exists on Chair Peak and on Cathedral Rock, two peaks 40 km apart in this same batch, and the
Cathedral Rock buttress is separately confused with its own 2003 variation. See _DEFECTS.
- 'Southeast Gully' on Guye Peak and 'South Gully/South Spur' on Guye Peak are different lines on different aspects, and
the South Gully additionally has TWO Mountain Project pages for its summer and winter forms with different grades and
different trailheads. Both forms are written here as separate variants rather than merged.
No time, distance or gain figure is averaged. Where two sources disagreed, the field is omitted. Where a base finding rests
on the DB row's own already-sourced enrichment rather than on a page read in this pass, _confidence says so in those words
and _sources is left EMPTY rather than filled with a URL that was not read.

approach_variants.name: Alpental and the Source Lake talus to the Chair snow patch, then the east face scree
approach_variants.season: Summer into autumn, once the snow patch below the face has shrunk and the rock is dry
approach_variants.notes:
From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, take the summer trail toward Source Lake. Where the trail meets the talus field, do NOT drop down — dropping is the turn for The Tooth. Instead hold your height and gain 100 to 200 horizontal feet until you can pass small cliff bands on your right. Above them the tread improves and runs just below a waterfall.

Leave the trail at a longer talus field, usually marked by a large cairn, and climb up and left on good paths between the talus to the permanent snow patch under the east face. Climb the snow patch to its top, then take the last 200 to 300 ft of loose scree, keeping hard against the base of the peak where the scree lies at a gentler angle.

Reckon two to three hours from the car to the foot of the route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LINE OF BOLTS IS THE TEST, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE YOU NEED IN CLOUD. This is a fully bolted alpine sport line. Every other route that starts on this side of Chair Peak is climbed on gear. If you cannot see a bolt from the ground, you are not at the start of this route, whatever the terrain looks like.

WHERE ALONG THE BASE: at the top of the scree there is a band of third and fourth class rock that guards the RIGHT-HAND side of Chair Peak. The route starts just past the LEFT edge of that band. So walk the base leftward until the guarding band ends, and the first bolted line past it is this one.

WHAT PITCH ONE FEELS LIKE, as confirmation: a few tricky moves straight off the ground at about 5.7, and then it eases into sustained, clean 5.6 slab for roughly 120 ft. Hard slab on clean rock with bolts is right. Broken blocky ground, or a chimney, is not.

HOW TO TELL IT FROM THE EAST FACE ROUTE, which is the mistake worth avoiding: the first-ascent party deliberately kept this line clear of the East Face, and the East Face both starts and finishes WELL TO THE RIGHT of it. So if you are at a gear start on broken rock, you have not walked far enough left along the base.

AND THE DESCENT GIVES YOU A BACK-BEARING: the ordinary Chair Peak gully descent lands you only about a hundred feet uphill of this route's base. A party coming down that gully that walks a hundred feet downhill is standing at the start.
hazards: The final 200-300 ft of approach scree is loose and sits directly under the face
A newer alpine line: loose pebbles and small rock still come off the upper pitches, and the last two pitches were left very dirty after cleaning
Several rappels leave under 5 ft of rope to spare on a 60m — knots in the ends are not optional
The eighth pitch must be belayed back down rather than rappelled, because rappelling it showers rock on anyone below
Parties stacked on the face: this and the East Face share the same descent gully

approach_variants.name: East face approach to Thumbtack Rock, then the grassy gully over the divide
approach_variants.season: Summer and autumn, once the ridge is free of snow
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the Northeast Buttress and east face approach from the Alpental lot: Snow Lake trail, the Source Lake fork, then the climbers' path and snow up the broad basin running southwest toward Chair's east face. About two hours in, that basin brings you to Thumbtack Rock, the small pinnacle every route on this side uses as its landmark.

At Thumbtack Rock the northwest ridge parts company with everything else. Turn RIGHT and climb a grassy gully that carries you over the ridge and around onto the northwest side, then head for the ridge itself.

About 4.8 km and roughly 3,100 ft of gain from the car to the top.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THUMBTACK ROCK IS THE DECISION POINT, AND THE TURN IS RIGHT AND UP A GRASSY GULLY. Everything else on this side of the mountain continues straight on up the basin to the foot of the east face. This route is the one that leaves at the Thumbtack and crosses the divide. A published fix for the Thumbtack is 10T 0616013E 5257415N. If you are still walking up the basin under a big east face, you have gone past the turn.

THE START ITSELF IS A SADDLE WITH TREES ON IT, and the first pitch goes up the gully to the LEFT of that saddle. Trees on a saddle, gully immediately left — that pairing is the arrival test, and both halves are visible from below in poor light.

CONFIRMATION ONE PITCH UP, which is the strongest signal on the route: pitch one runs about 200 ft to the crest and you belay off trees on the SOUTH side of the ridge. From those trees you scramble down and left to a chimney-shaped feature with a CHOCKSTONE jammed at its top. You cannot see that chockstone from the trees; it becomes obvious as soon as you scramble across. A chockstone-capped chimney at the end of a short downward scramble means you are on the northwest ridge and nothing else.

NEGATIVE TESTS: if your first pitch is bolted, you are on Voie de Chaise on the east face. If you are looking up at a big buttress from the head of the basin, you never made the Thumbtack turn.
hazards: Poor, broken rock and runout ridge climbing — the route's own reputation is that the setting beats the climbing
A hard-to-protect move on a small vertical face of poor rock above the chockstone
Exposure on both sides of a narrow crest
A descent that goes SOUTH over false summits to find a rappel tree in the SECOND gully east — the first gully you meet is not it
Fixed rappel gear on the descent has been found set for snow conditions and out of reach on dry rock

approach_variants.name: Alpental and the Northeast Buttress approach, then round onto the slabs on the west side
approach_variants.season: Spring into mid-summer while the slabs still hold snow that can be crossed; a light axe and light crampons are the usual kit until midsummer, after which it goes on dry rock
approach_variants.notes:
Use the standard Chair Peak trailhead at Alpental, the same start the Northeast Buttress uses. From the basin, traverse slabby ground round onto the west side of the peak. Early in the season that slab traverse holds snow and can be cut by glide cracks, which is the part of this approach worth respecting rather than the walking.

Roughly two to two and a half hours from the parking area to the foot of the route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE LOOKING FOR THE BOTTOM OF A NARROW COULOIR, NOT FOR THE CREST. The route does not start on the ridge. It starts up a narrow couloir about 220 ft long that delivers you to the LOW POINT of the west ridge, and only then does the climbing follow the crest.

THE TOWER IS THE MARKER. That low point sits immediately EAST of a distinct tower on the ridge. So find the tower, look east of it for the lowest saddle in the skyline, and the couloir is the direct line beneath that saddle. Tower on your left as you look up the couloir, low point of the ridge at its top: that is the start.

WHAT THE FIRST TWO PITCHES SHOULD FEEL LIKE: two pitches of 5.7 in the gully to reach the top of it. If the couloir tops out on ground that is obviously not the lowest gap on the ridge, you are in the wrong gully and you will meet the tower rather than the ridge above it.

WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, since this is the commonest gross error here: the standard descent for Chair Peak runs down a couloir on the SOUTH side into a narrow rappel gully. That is a different feature and it is a way down, not this route's way up. If you are on the side you approached from and staring at the east face, you have not gone round far enough.
hazards: Early-season snow on the slab traverse, with glide cracks opening in it
Loose rock along the ridge crest
Sections of the crest with little available protection
The descent couloir on the south side funnels into the same narrow rappel gully every other Chair Peak route uses, so expect traffic above you

wa_chair_peak_west_ridge._confidence: row-derived: the DB row's own Pro Guiding-sourced description is the only published account of this line found; the couloir/tower/low-point sequence comes from it and was not independently corroborated

approach_variants.name: Alpental to Pineapple Pass, then west along the base past The Tooth Fairy
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to September on dry rock; the approach gully to Pineapple Pass holds snow into early summer and an axe is worth carrying then
approach_variants.notes:
Take the Snow Lake trail from Alpental, fork toward Source Lake, cross the talus and climb the steep gully to Pineapple Pass — the standard approach every route on this side of The Tooth shares.

From the pass, keep going LEFT (west), past the foot of The Tooth Fairy, and continue along the base of the cliff. The route is a bolted line, so the walk is over ground the other routes here have already made obvious.

About 4.8 km and 2,700 ft to the summit.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT OFF FROM THE TOOTH FAIRY AND FIND THE GULLY. This route starts roughly 500 ft climbers' LEFT of The Tooth Fairy, and the feature that fixes it is a LARGE GULLY THAT SPLITS THE CLIFF. The route takes the LEFT-HAND SIDE of that gully. So: Tooth Fairy behind you on the right, big cleaving gully in front of you, start on its left wall.

THE HARDWARE TEST, which works in any visibility: this is an all-bolt line. Quickdraws and nothing else. If you are pulling out cams to protect the first moves, you are on one of the peak's trad routes, not on this one.

THE FIRST-PITCH GRADE TEST: pitch one goes at 5.9 to 5.10a, with an easier 5.8 alternative start bolted to the RIGHT. If the first pitch is going at 5.4 you are round on the South Face; if it feels like broken fourth-class scrambling you have not left Pineapple Pass.

AND A CONFIRMATION HIGHER UP FOR A PARTY THAT WANTS ONE: the third pitch CROSSES THE GULLY on a large chockstone, and the fourth pitch takes a V-slot at 5.10b. Crossing that gully mid-route on a chockstone is the signature of this line.

FINALLY, WHERE IT PUTS YOU: the last bolted anchor is not the summit. One more bolt above it leads onto the North Ridge and about 100 m of unprotected scrambling to the true top. A route whose bolts run out at the summit is not this one.
hazards: About 100 m of unprotected third and fourth class scrambling on the North Ridge above the last bolt to reach the true summit
An all-bolt sport line on an alpine peak, with alpine weather and no quick escape
Parties on the South Face and Tooth Fairy above and beside you sharing one descent
The approach gully to Pineapple Pass holds snow into early summer

approach_variants.name: Standard Tooth approach, but break off north of the Pineapple Pass gully
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to September, once the approach snow has gone; heavy weekend traffic in that window
approach_variants.notes:
From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, follow the Snow Lake trail about a mile and a half, fork toward Source Lake, cross the talus and start up toward Pineapple Pass on the standard line.

The difference is at the top. Do NOT finish the gully to the pass. Break off to the NORTH of it and climb the open books on the face above instead. This is the route parties take when the South Face is backed up, and it is deliberately the path of least resistance between The Tooth Fairy and the South Face.

About 4.8 km and 2,500 ft from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A THING YOU DO NOT DO: DO NOT GO UP TO PINEAPPLE PASS. Hike the stable talus toward the pass and then leave it, heading NORTH of the gully that finishes at the pass. If you have stood in the notch at Pineapple Pass, you have overshot the start of this route and you are at the start of the South Face.

WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR ON THE ROCK: OPEN BOOKS. Pitches one and two climb open-book corners that begin north of the Pineapple Pass gully, and they lead to a LEFT-FACING SLAB. Corner, corner, then slab facing left. That sequence is the confirmation, and none of it requires seeing the summit.

AND A THIRD-PITCH CHECK IF YOU ARE STILL UNSURE: pitch three finds THREE CRACKS running up to an overhang, and the route face-climbs to the LEFT of those three cracks. Three cracks under a roof, and you go left of them. If you are climbing the cracks themselves you have drifted right.

HOW IT DIFFERS FROM ITS TWO NEIGHBOURS: The Tooth Fairy is further left again and goes at 5.9; the South Face starts from the notch at the top of the pass at 5.4. This route sits between them, both physically and in difficulty, at 5.5. If your first pitch feels like 5.9, you have gone too far left.

A WARNING THAT BELONGS WITH THE FINDING: this face is loose, and it sits above the popular routes. Being on the correct start also means being above other people.
hazards: Loose blocks on the open-book corner pitches
The route sits directly above the busy South Face — rockfall onto parties below is the documented concern here, not just a generic one
Rockfall risk to and from routes sharing the approach gully and the summit area
Descent route-finding: the broken west and north side offers several plausible gullies, and the loose east-side gully should not be rappelled

approach_variants.name: Alpental into the basin below the east face, avoiding the summer gully in winter
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, and only when the upper mixed ground has built up enough snow and ice to climb and protect — first climbed in winter 1995 and genuinely condition-dependent
approach_variants.notes:
From the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead at about 3,100 ft, hike or skin toward Source Lake, then turn south into the basin beneath The Tooth's east face.

In winter, do not use the summer approach path and gully that run directly below the east face. That line is avalanche terrain and the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is the pre-trip read, not an optional one. Take the broader basin instead and come at the face from open ground.

About 3.2 km and 2,500 ft to the top.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE STARTS ON THE SUMMER EAST FACE, SO FINDING THE EAST FACE IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM, AND THE ANSWER IS TO GO PAST THE SOUTH FACE START. From the notch at the top of Pineapple Pass, where the South Face begins, walk RIGHT (north) along the base, underneath the east face. That is the published direction and it is a walk, not a climb.

WHAT THE FIRST TWO PITCHES SHOULD FEEL LIKE: fourth class to about 5.5, on sub-par rock with tricky protection. Easy ground that is hard to protect is right for this face. If pitch one is clean and well protected you are somewhere else on the mountain.

THE MOVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM THE SUMMER ROUTE, and the point at which you will know for certain: after roughly two pitches on the summer line, this variation TRAVERSES LEFT about 30 ft, with little protection on the traverse, into a corner sitting below a steep rock barrier. That corner is the crux — 5.8-ish with one aid move, or M5 when it is iced. A leftward traverse into a corner under a barrier means you are on the variation; carrying straight on up means you are on the summer East Face.

AND THE FINISH CONFIRMS IT: the last pitch is steep SNOW, belayed off small trees, trending slightly right to finish near the summit. A rock finish is the summer route.

HONEST LIMIT: sources describe this line in these blocks rather than pitch by pitch. If the ice is not there, there is no route to find, and that is a real answer rather than a route-finding failure.
hazards: Avalanche danger in the Source Lake basin and specifically in the summer gully below the east face — take the broad basin in winter
PG13: sustained runout climbing on marginal protection with real injury potential
Rockfall from above onto the east face
Steep unconsolidated snow on the final pitch, prone to sloughing
The descent is the South Face rappel line, shared with other parties, on a short winter day

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
approach_variants.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far LEFT until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIFFS ARE THE MARKER, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS TO OVERSHOOT THEM BY 100 FT. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further LEFT past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

WHAT CONFIRMS IT ONCE YOU ARE IN: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the FIRST CHOCKSTONE, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A SECOND chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

THE EXIT TEST FOR LATER: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn LEFT before the gully ends — look for TWO LARGE TREES and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

AND ONE DESCENT WARNING THAT PARTIES GET WRONG: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the MIDDLE summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite with a documented fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit

approach_variants.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY IS THE OBVIOUS ONE ON THE SOUTH SIDE, AND THE TEST IS THAT IT FORCES YOU OUT LEFT. Walk round the south side until you are under the single obvious gully cleaving it. That is the whole identification at ground level; there is no second candidate on this aspect.

THE CONFIRMATION IS THE CHOCKSTONE, AND IT COMES EARLY. Scramble the gully until one or two chockstones jammed in it stop you and force you climbers' LEFT out onto the adjacent face for a short section before you regain the gully and follow the South Spur. If you can walk the gully to its top without ever being pushed onto the face, you are not in the right one.

WHAT THE ROCK SHOULD FEEL LIKE: easy fifth class at most, protected by a small rack and slung trees, with parties sometimes rigging a hand line over the exposed ground above the chockstones. Anything sustained or steep is not this route.

AND THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST ITS NEIGHBOURS: the big WEST face and the South Rib are separate features on other aspects. If you are looking at a large clean wall rather than into a vegetated cleft, you are round on the west side.
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall is very likely and the peak has a documented history of fatalities from rockfall and breaking holds
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully — helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant rather than technical
Access: private property on the walking approach, closed to climbers

approach_variants.name: Old Commonwealth Basin trail to a bearing of 290 degrees, then straight up
approach_variants.season: Winter and early spring, roughly January to April, when the gully is filled and consolidated. The ideal is a cold night followed by a clear cold morning; by late spring the sunlit half turns to slush and the route becomes a wet-avalanche problem
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Pacific Crest Trail North / Snoqualmie Pass North trailhead at about 47.4284, -121.4155, just off I-90 exit 52. Follow the old Commonwealth Basin trail north for roughly 1.4 miles, or the bootpack that stands in for it in winter.

When Guye lies directly west or northwest of you, leave the trail and go straight up the slope. The walking is short by Cascade standards; the difficulty is judging the snow on the slope between the trail and the gully, which is itself avalanche terrain on a loaded day.

About 2.25 km and 2,100 ft of gain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TAKE A BEARING, BECAUSE THIS ONE CAN BE DONE BLIND. Walk the old Commonwealth Basin trail about 1.4 miles until the summit of Guye bears roughly 290 degrees — west-northwest — from you, then turn and go straight uphill. A published fix for the start of the route is about 47.4411, -121.4026. In cloud that pair of numbers settles it and nothing on the ground has to be seen.

WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO, IN ORDER, ONCE YOU COMMIT: the route starts by going 45 degrees straight up. Only then does the gully proper develop, turning NORTHWEST for about 40 m and steepening as it turns. After that it runs directly at the summit, which stays visible for much of the climb on a clear day. If the ground you are on stays uniformly angled and never turns northwest, you are on the open slope beside the gully rather than in it.

THE ANGLE IS THE OTHER TEST: this is the steepest of Guye's gully lines. About 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then progressively steeper, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. A gully that stays moderate all the way is one of the peak's other lines.

WHERE IT PUTS YOU: it finishes at the ridge between the TRUE and FALSE summits — not on a summit. If your line tops out on a summit block, it is not this one.

AND A CONDITIONS TEST THAT IS PART OF THE FINDING HERE: roughly half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which is what gives it solid snow under the surface. It also means the two halves can be in quite different condition on a warm day.
hazards: Avalanche is the primary objective hazard — a confined gully below a summit ridge on a slope that loads readily
Sustained steep snow to about 70 degrees with essentially no protection; a fall in the upper section is unarrestable
Cornice formation at the exit onto the ridge between the true and false summits
Rapid sun-warming of the exposed half producing wet slides and rollerballs later in the day
Both descents — Cave Ridge west, Commonwealth east — cross avalanche terrain of their own, and the west bootpath is easily lost under snow

approach_variants.name: Alpental lot, boot path east along the base of the South Rib
approach_variants.season: Roughly May to October. This south-facing crag low on the mountain dries early and stays dry late, but it bakes on a hot midsummer afternoon — mornings and shoulder seasons climb better
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road off I-90 exit 52. Take the boot path and old ski track up from the lot and traverse EAST along the base of Guye Peak's South Rib. The crag is passed on that traverse; it is roughly half a mile of walking and about 15 minutes, not an approach in any real sense.

This is a single 50 ft pitch that does not top out, so it is a crag visit rather than a mountain day.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU CAN SEE THE CRAG FROM THE CAR PARK, AND THAT IS THE ANSWER IN BAD WEATHER. The cliff is visible from the west-most parking lots at the Summit West base area. Look at it from the road before you walk in, fix which lump of rock it is, and the walk becomes trivial.

WHERE IT SITS RELATIVE TO THE PEAK: it is an isolated crag, separate from the rest of Guye, low down and near the base of the South Rib. If you are looking at the large WEST FACE, this cliff is just around the corner to the RIGHT of it and well below. So: west face on your left shoulder, corner, small isolated cliff low on the right.

THE MOVE OFF THE GROUND IS THE PROOF, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE. The pitch starts steeply off a LEFT-HAND SIDE-PULL, and the first piece is a #1 Camalot plugged into a POD, before you clip the first bolt. If there is no pod at head height taking a #1 and no bolt above it, you are at the wrong bit of rock.

AND THE SHAPE OF THE WHOLE THING, as a final check: 50 ft, a rest ledge partway up, then a pumpy sequence moving left to a TWO-BOLT CHAIN ANCHOR. It does not top out. Any line here that continues into the mountain above is not this route.

HONEST CAVEAT: this is a 2014 line with almost no recorded traffic, so the fixed gear is aging and seldom inspected.
hazards: Rockfall from the South Rib and the loose slopes above the crag
Aging, seldom-inspected fixed hardware on a route with almost no recorded traffic
Poor rock quality typical of Guye Peak's fractured rhyolite even on a bolted line
South aspect low on the mountain bakes on hot afternoons

approach_variants.name: Alpental groomer lot, the Phantom Slide, and the NW shoulder notch into Thunder Creek cirque
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to March. A sustained cold snap usually gives the fattest ice; warm or dry winters leave it thin and force dry-tooling
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the groomer lot about 200 ft past the main Alpental day lot. Walk up the open south-facing hillside toward the Alpental waterfalls. At the foot of the falls, cut LEFT into the trees for roughly 100 ft and climb through two steep, usually snowed-up cliff bands. After about 300 ft of gain, move back RIGHT onto the Phantom Slide.

The Phantom Slide is a broad avalanche path that slides regularly, including on people on the upper apron. Check the NWAC forecast and time the crossing rather than lingering on it.

Climb the slide to about 4,900 ft, then trend up and left through more open ground to a notch on the northwest shoulder near 5,200 ft. Reckon roughly one and a half to three hours car to base, and much of that depends on whether a skin track already exists — most of the approach is through thick trees.

No water on this approach in winter; melt snow.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE NOTCH, DOWNCLIMB ABOUT 200 VERTICAL FEET AND TRAVERSE TO THE FIRST OBVIOUS GULLY. That is the published test and it is the one that works in cloud, because it is counted rather than seen: you are not identifying a gully by its shape from a distance, you are walking beneath the face from a fixed point and taking the first one you meet.

WHY THAT MATTERS HERE MORE THAN ANYWHERE ELSE ON THIS PAGE: this face carries FIVE closely spaced ice and mixed lines — Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully and LA Express — and they are near enough together that racking up under the wrong one is the normal failure. Count from the notch, do not pick by appearance.

THE PITCH-ONE CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS A GOOD ONE: ascend roughly 200 ft up the gully and then take an OBVIOUS RAMP OUT TO THE LEFT, belaying from a quasi-cave. Gully, then a left-trending ramp, then a cave belay. If your first rope length does not offer a left ramp at about 200 ft, you are in a neighbouring line.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS HIGHER AND UNAMBIGUOUS: the route runs up obvious weaknesses to a SMALL HEADWALL split by a 5.8 CRACK, historically aided and now freed. That crack is the route's signature. A line with no headwall crack is not New York Gully.

AND A HONEST WARNING ABOUT THE APPROACH ITSELF: most of it is through thick timber and the published advice is to go with somebody who knows it or follow an existing skin track. Without a track, expect it to be slow and to be the part of the day where you lose time.
hazards: The Phantom Slide is an active avalanche path and the approach crosses and climbs it
Five closely spaced lines on one face — racking up below the wrong one is the routine error
Loose, chossy rock on pitch two and through the box gully
Thin or absent ice most winters; be ready to dry-tool rather than swing
A cold, shaded northwest aspect with winter temperatures at the belays even on clear days
Alpental ski patrol conducts explosive avalanche control nearby
The descent finishes down the Southwest Slopes scramble, itself 3,100 ft of steep loose ground, or back down the Phantom Slide

approach_variants.name: The unsigned boot path 50 ft below the Snow Lake trailhead sign
approach_variants.season: Late July to September for a snow-free scramble; the upper gully commonly holds snow into July. Also climbed as a winter and spring snow route by parties competent to assess avalanche danger
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road; a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the kiosk.

Walk toward the signed Snow Lake trailhead but do not take that trail. About 50 ft DOWNHILL (south) of the Snow Lake sign, an unsigned boot path and old roadbed drops into a band of slide alder. That is the shared start for both Guye Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain.

The path steepens at once and follows the Source Creek drainage through roots, talus and brush. At roughly a mile and 1,000 ft of gain a junction splits — the RIGHT fork goes to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge, and the Snoqualmie route continues left and straight. A third of a mile past that the path fords the creek by a 50 ft waterfall, the main water on route. A quarter mile beyond the crossing it breaks out of the trees onto the open west-facing slope below Cave Ridge and switchbacks up it for the final mile.

About 3.8 miles round trip with 3,100 ft of gain, though sources differ on where the mileage is measured from.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH IS THE ROUTE HERE, SO THE FINDING IS ABOUT THREE JUNCTIONS RATHER THAN A CLIFF, AND EACH ONE HAS A PHYSICAL MARKER.

FIRST, THE START: 50 ft DOWNHILL of the Snow Lake trailhead sign, into slide alder. It is an old roadbed, not a trail, and it is easy to walk straight past. If you are on wide, well-graded tread you are on the Snow Lake trail and you are on the wrong path from the first step.

SECOND, THE FORK AT ABOUT A MILE AND 1,000 FT: right goes to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge, left and straight is Snoqualmie. Getting this wrong puts you on a different mountain, and it is the junction where parties most often go astray.

THIRD, THE WATERFALL: about a third of a mile past that fork the path fords the creek beside a roughly 50 ft waterfall. Crossing beside a waterfall is confirmation you are still on the Snoqualmie line, and it is the last reliable water.

AND THE SUMMIT ITSELF HAS A TRAP WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU GET THERE: the trail-accessible summit is not the true one. A rugged pinnacle roughly 550 horizontal feet EAST was resurveyed in 2023 as about 3 ft higher, and reaching it needs an exposed fourth-class step. A party that walks to the top and stops has stopped 3 ft short, deliberately or not.
hazards: A steep, loose, unmaintained climbers' path — easy to kick rock onto a party below
Snow lingering in the upper gully and switchbacks into July; an axe and the skill to use it may be needed
An exposed fourth-class step to reach the true east summit
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes in winter and spring, with ski patrol control work nearby
The descent is looser and harder to control than the ascent; the gully funnels into trees and rock lower down, which matters if you glissade

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route._confidence: row-derived: the 50-ft-below-the-sign start, the Guye fork and the waterfall ford come from the DB row's own sourced approach text

approach_variants.name: Alpental base area and the ski runs under the old Armstrong Express line
approach_variants.season: Late spring to mid-July, after the resort closes but before the snow gullies melt out and expose looser rock and scree
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the large Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road, about 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead and no maintained trail for Denny Mountain. Cross the base area and pick up boot tracks and climbers' paths on the north-facing slopes under the old Armstrong Express and Sessel chair lines.

On snow this is simple: walk the barren lower slopes a few hundred feet to snowline, put on crampons and axe, and follow the Lower International run into a small basin, then the steep Upper International run — a double-black pitch that holds firm snow late and is the crux in spring — to the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station.

Dry, the same line is a rough boot path and scree scramble through slide alder, small hemlocks and huckleberry, with only intermittent flagging that does not reliably mark anything.

About 2.5 to 2.8 miles and 2,500 ft one way.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS PEAK GIVES YOU MAN-MADE LANDMARKS, WHICH IS UNUSUAL AND WORTH USING. Navigate by the ski runs and the lift, not by the mountain: Lower International, then the steep Upper International, then the TOP OF THE EDELWEISS CHAIRLIFT UNLOADING STATION. Standing at that lift station is the arrival test for the end of the approach, and it is a building — it does not disappear in cloud.

WHERE THE REAL CLIMBING BEGINS: above the lift station, angle up the WIDE OPEN RAMP toward the summit horn, which changes underfoot from scree and heather to broken rock.

THE UNMISTAKABLE MARKER IS A FIXED STEEL CABLE. A short via-ferrata-style handline protects an exposed, down-sloping and often slick ledge traverse just below the top. There is nothing else like it on this mountain. If you have reached steep ground and there is no cable, you are not on the correct line to the summit block.

AND THE TOP CONFIRMS ITSELF: past the cable, a short class 2-3 scramble through a NARROW ROCK CLEFT reaches a summit carrying an old radio-relay structure and a survey marker. Hardware on the summit is the final proof.

THE HARD PART, HONESTLY STATED: on dry ground the route-finding LOW on the mountain is the hazard, not the summit. The flagging is pink, white and blue, inconsistent, and does not reliably mark the line. In snow this problem disappears entirely, which is why the season here is spring rather than summer.
hazards: Loose footing on scree and dirt once the snow has gone
Neck-deep slide alder and bramble low on the mountain in summer, with unreliable flagging
Ski-area infrastructure on the route
A brief exposed class 2-3 step and narrow ledge at the true summit
Avalanche terrain on these slopes when snow-covered

wa_denny_mountain_north_slopes._confidence: row-derived: the ski-run, Edelweiss lift-station and fixed-cable sequence comes from the DB row's own sourced approach text; no independent route page was retrieved for this line

approach_variants.name: Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the gully splitting Bryant's southeast face
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
approach_variants.notes:
From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits LEFT (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col.

Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face.

Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.

About 9.5 miles round trip and on the order of 3,000 to 3,400 ft of gain; four to six hours trailhead to summit for a fit party.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE THUMBTACK IS THE LANDMARK YOU WALK PAST, AND THE GULLY IS THE ONE IMMEDIATELY BEYOND IT. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

WHAT THE GULLY IS, IN OTHER WORDS: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

THE FOOTING TEST TELLS YOU WHERE TO BE WITHIN IT: climb favouring the FAR CLIMBERS' RIGHT side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

WHERE IT DELIVERS YOU: the gully tops out on the BRYANT-CHAIR CONNECTING RIDGE, not on a summit. From there you work SOUTH over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. A gully that finishes on a summit is not this one.

AND THE LAST STEP CHANGES CHARACTER WITH THE SNOW, which is worth knowing before you commit: with snow on the block the final scramble is easy class 3 with little real exposure. Dry, the only reasonable line goes round the NORTH — climbers' left — side on exposed and distinctly loose class 3. Test every hold.
hazards: The gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring; avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm
Loose scree, with the centre and left of the gully markedly worse than the right
The gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow, requiring axe and crampons
Exposed and loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when the block is dry

wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes._confidence: row-derived: the Thumbtack talus, the gully and the climbers'-right footing rule come from the DB row's own sourced approach; the MP Bryant Peak area page confirms the peak and its position on the Chair connecting ridge

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Rock Trail to the pass, then a rising traverse under the east face
approach_variants.season: July to September. The northeast side is shaded and dries slowly, so give it time after rain and expect approach snow into July
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 80 at Cle Elum, take SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald along Cle Elum Lake for about 14.8 miles, then gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 for 12.3 miles and the short NF-153 spur to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, Trail #1345, at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free self-issue wilderness permit.

The trail climbs through old growth to Nosh Nosh Wahtum, formerly Squaw Lake, at about 4,850 ft and 2.5 miles, then opens into meadow with Cathedral Rock ahead. At about 4 miles you reach Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft and the PCT junction.

Walk north on the PCT for a couple of minutes, then cut across the meadow to a stand of trees. Parties cache the gear they do not need on the climb there. From the trees, start a rising traverse under the east face, past the meadows, and then across a loose talus slope with the northeast buttress in sight.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE TOP OF A SHORT, STEEP SNOWFIELD, AND THAT SNOWFIELD IS THE ARRIVAL TEST. Crossing the loose talus under the east face you come to it; it is short but steep enough that parties in approach shoes have picked their way up it holding stones for security. Reaching the top of that snow patch is reaching the start of the climbing.

AND HERE IS THE MISTAKE PARTIES ACTUALLY MAKE AT THAT POINT, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN THIS ENTRY: at the top of the snow it is natural to exit RIGHT onto ledges and start up from there. That is wrong. A party that does it finds the ground harder than the fourth class the description promises, wanders left, right and up, and comes back down. The correct start is to exit back LEFT into the MOAT at the top of the snow, where the terrain is much easier.

SO THE TEST IS A DIFFICULTY TEST: if your first moves off the snow feel harder than fourth class, you are on the wrong side of the snowfield. Go back and take the moat on the left.

WHAT SHOULD FOLLOW: easy ground you can simul-climb, then a LEDGE SYSTEM that traverses RIGHTWARD toward the crest of the buttress. Beckey gives the buttress seven pitches, about 900 ft, at 5.7 and grade III. A route that is sustained from the first pitch is not it.

AND ONE THING TO SETTLE BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE TREES: this peak is descended by the SOUTH side, not by reversing the buttress. Note where you came up.
hazards: Loose, fractured andesite throughout — poor and unpredictable protection on every technical route on this peak
A short steep snowfield with loose and sharp rock below it, crossed by parties in approach shoes
The moat at the top of the snow
Rockfall down the gully systems from parties, wind and thaw
Descent route-finding on the shattered south and southwest flanks, where many plausible gullies cliff out
Summer convection over the Cascade crest, on an exposed tower with no cell coverage and a remote trailhead

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass, the gear-cache trees, and the traverse to the original route's first pitch
approach_variants.season: Late July to September. Late August and September give the driest rock and the coldest, most stable air, which is worth waiting for where the protection is already marginal
approach_variants.notes:
Drive and hike as for the Northeast Buttress: Trail #1345 from the Cathedral Rock trailhead at about 3,350 ft, past Nosh Nosh Wahtum at 2.5 miles, to Cathedral Pass and the PCT junction at 5,550 ft and 4 miles. Sign the wilderness permit at the register.

Cut across the meadow to the stand of trees — the usual gear cache — and traverse under the east face across talus to the northeast side.

This variation does not have its own start on the ground: it begins where the ORIGINAL Northeast Ridge route finishes its first pitch. Mountain Project sends climbers to Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide for that original start.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR: THIS ROUTE'S BASE IS THE TOP OF SOMEBODY ELSE'S FIRST PITCH. You find the original Northeast Ridge start — the short steep snowfield on the northeast side, exiting LEFT into the moat rather than right onto the harder ledges — climb its first pitch, and only then are you at the beginning of the 2003 line.

THE FEATURE THAT PROVES YOU ARE ON THE VARIATION AND NOT ON THE ORIGINAL, and this is the one to memorise, is YELLOW-SPECKLED ROCK. From the top of that first pitch, traverse LEFT and up over a short pitch of genuinely unstable class 4+ ground, aiming for a LEFT-HAND VERTICAL CRACK in a LEFT-FACING CORNER, identified by yellow-speckled rock with ROOFS ABOVE IT. Yellow speckles plus roofs above a left-facing corner is the target; nothing else on this side of the peak reads that way.

THE CONFIRMATION IS THE THIRD PITCH: it climbs that crack and exits over its LEFT side. It is the best pitch on the route, 5.7 to 5.8 and well protected — which is worth knowing precisely because everything below it is not. If pitch three is poorly protected choss, you are not in the corner you wanted.

A HIGHER CHECK: above, the rock eases, and a short difficult LEFT-LEANING CRACK at 5.9+ comes before moderate terrain to the summit.

AND THE HONEST WARNING THAT BELONGS IN A BASE FINDING HERE: the pitch you must cross to reach the good climbing is described by the first-ascent party as scary and unstable. Its own Mountain Project rating is PG13, and the route would carry more stars if not for that second pitch. Knowing that in advance is what stops a party assuming they are off route when the ground feels wrong.
hazards: Shattered, friable andesite giving loose holds and unreliable protection
An explicitly unstable class 4+ section low on the route that must be crossed to reach the good climbing
PG13 protection with significant fall consequences
Rockfall onto belayers from a ridge littered with loose blocks
Six pitches at 5.9 plus a route-finding descent make benightment a real risk on a short day
No cell coverage and a remote gravel-access trailhead: slow rescue

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
approach_variants.season: Best while Pea Soup Lake is still frozen and the moat is closed. The Pea Soup approach becomes problematic from mid-July onward once the ice melts
approach_variants.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do NOT follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse BELOW the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A LAKE YOU WALK ACROSS. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to FROZEN PEA SOUP LAKE. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

WHAT TO DO WHEN THE LAKE HAS MELTED OUT, WHICH IS THE COMMON CASE FROM MID-JULY: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge SEPARATING the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the FIRST MINOR NOTCH at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' LEFT via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

GETTING ONTO THE ICE, IN EITHER SEASON: early, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT. Late, bypass on climbers' LEFT by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

AND THE TOP TELLS YOU WHICH SUMMIT IS WHICH: the glacier leads to the GAP BETWEEN THE TWO HIGHEST SUMMITS. From the notch, the WEST summit — on your RIGHT — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A SCOPE NOTE THAT MATTERS TO PEAK-LIST PARTIES: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.
hazards: Full-width crevasses opening late in the season across the Lynch Glacier
Loose, rotten rock on the ground used to gain and leave the ice — reported as the worst hazard on the route
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition that widens through the summer
Pea Soup Lake melting out and Lynch draw flooding from mid-July
Significant glacier recession, so old descriptions understate the rock and moat work

approach_variants.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
approach_variants.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
approach_variants.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse WEST to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AIMING FOR THE OUTLET OF PEA SOUP LAKE, AND THE SHOULDER ABOVE THE FOSS RIVER IS THE WAYPOINT THAT GETS YOU THERE. From Dip Top Gap the traverse is WEST until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. If you are looking down into a drainage that is not the Foss, you have not traversed far enough west.

FROM THE OUTLET THE FINDING IS THE SAME AS FROM PEGGY'S POND: get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS at the head of the lake. Early season, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT; late season, bypass by class 3 on climbers' LEFT and cross the moat. Then ascend the upper glacier toward the West Pyramid and the col between the Middle and True summits.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: this route is graded third class with only minor snow and ice difficulty. If you are on steep ice, you are not on the Lynch Glacier standard line.
hazards: Crevasses across the full width of the glacier late in the season
The moat at the rock-to-ice transition
Loose rotten rock on the class 3 bypass
A long approach over Dip Top Gap with a descent to the lake that must be reversed on the way out

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass, the ledge traverse to Peggy's Pond, and the Southeast Ridge
approach_variants.season: July to September. Snow can linger above the pond well into July and an axe is worth carrying then
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cathedral Rock / Deception Pass trailhead at the end of FR-4330, about 3,400 ft, take the signed Deception Pass / Cathedral Pass trail. At about 1.8 miles a signed junction splits right to Squaw Lake — stay left. The trail climbs another two miles into subalpine meadow and switchbacks to Cathedral Pass at about 5,500 ft and 4.2 to 4.5 miles, at the PCT junction.

From the pass drop briefly toward Deep Lake on the PCT; a use path leaves at a switchback toward Peggy's Pond, or continue to the signed Peggy's Pond Trail #1375 junction. Either way the last half mile is a rough, primitive traverse across narrow ledges with real exposure to steep drop-offs. Go slowly with a pack; it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail.

Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft, five to five and a half miles in, is the last reliable water and the last established camp.

About 12 km and 5,100 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH HAS A HARD EDGE AND IT IS THE LEDGE TRAVERSE INTO PEGGY'S POND. That half-mile of narrow ledges with exposure is the last thing between trail and mountain, and it is the point at which a party knows it has left the walking behind. Peggy's Pond is the base camp and the last water.

FROM THE POND, THE FINDING IS AN ALTITUDE AND A SHAPE: braided boot paths head northwest then west across heather benches and talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft over about a mile, to the broad SOUTHEAST RIDGE at 6,800 to 7,000 ft. You are on the right ridge when it NARROWS WESTWARD with the HYAS CREEK GLACIER ON YOUR RIGHT and CIRCLE LAKE FAR BELOW ON YOUR LEFT. That pairing — glacier right, lake left — is the confirmation, and it does not need the summit to be visible.

THE NEXT CHECKPOINT IS A SADDLE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT between the East and Middle summits, reached by traversing climbers' trail and open scree BELOW the East Summit at 7,899 ft. The path is faint where it first leaves the ridge and well defined afterwards, so a faint start is not evidence you are off route.

WHERE THE GLACIER COMES IN: to use the Daniel Glacier proper, enter it just NORTH of a prominent spire on the Northeast Ridge and traverse west across it to the Middle Summit.

AND THE ONE THING NOT TO DO NEAR THE TOP: the true West Summit at 7,960 ft is reached over loose talus, lingering snowfields and the rocky margin of the Daniel Glacier remnant. Stay on the rock and scree spine. Wandering onto the glacier ice on the north side is where the crevasses are.
hazards: An exposed, primitive ledge traverse into Peggy's Pond, harder than the trail that precedes it
An early creek crossing near the trailhead that can be a wet ford in high water
Loose talus and route-finding uncertainty below the East Summit
Real crevasses opening on the Daniel and Lynch glacier ice on the north side by late summer
Lingering snow into July that can require an axe on the slopes above the pond

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley to La Bohn Gap and the lakes
approach_variants.season: July to September. Most parties make it a two or three day trip
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Necklace Valley trailhead at about 1,650 ft at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first five miles are deceptively flat, gaining only about 600 ft along the East Fork Foss River, entering the wilderness at about 1.5 miles.

Around mile 5 the trail FORDS the East Fork Foss River — there is no bridge and it runs high and cold in early-season melt, so cross in the morning at low flow. Then it turns uphill in earnest, roughly 2,400 ft over three miles of steep, root-laced switchbacks. This is the real crux of the approach for tired legs.

The grade eases at Jade Lake at about 4,600 ft and eight to nine miles, then Emerald and Opal Lakes through the swampy Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water, buggy in early summer.

From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends. Continue cross-country on an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus, up and east roughly a mile to a mile and a half and over 1,000 ft, to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes. That is the standard high camp: about 10 to 11 miles one way with over 5,000 ft of cumulative gain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LA BOHN GAP AND ITS LAKES ARE THE ARRIVAL, AND THE HONEST FINDING IS THAT THERE IS NO LONGER MUCH OF A GLACIER TO FIND. Measured in August 2022, the Hinman Glacier had largely disappeared, leaving stranded patches of snow and ice. So do not stand at the gap looking for a glacier front to identify. What you are looking for is the basin above the gap: mostly bare rock and permanent snowfield in most recent seasons, with crevasse and bergschrund hazard only in early season or after a big snow year.

HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT LA BOHN GAP: it is where the cairned climbers' path out of the head of Necklace Basin tops out at over 5,500 ft, with the La Bohn Lakes in it. If you are still in swampy lake-studded basin on maintained tread, you have not left Necklace Valley.

WHICH WAY FROM THE GAP, AND THE TWO SOURCES DISAGREE, SO CARRY BOTH: the DB row's own approach text says the route continues NORTH from La Bohn Gap onto the glacier basin, while the Mountaineers route description says ascend EAST from La Bohn Lakes to the Hinman Glacier. Both agree the objective is the snowfield basin immediately above the lakes and that easy class 2 ridge and scree ground leads from it to the summit ridge. Do not average them; look for the basin, which is unmistakable once you are at the gap.

THE FINAL TEST IS A DISTANCE ALONG A RIDGE: from where you gain the summit ridge, the true summit at 7,492 ft is about HALF A MILE along it. A party that tops out on the ridge and stops is half a mile short.
hazards: An unbridged ford of the East Fork Foss River around mile 5, high and cold in early-season melt
2,400 ft of steep root-laced switchbacks with a multi-day pack
Crevasse and bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant, mostly early season
Loose rock on the final class 2 scramble
Mosquitoes in the lake basins in early and mid summer
A long walk out from a remote camp if anything goes wrong

approach_variants.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the basin, then the lowest notch on the west ridge
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the PCT North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft: cross under I-90, take the first right, lot on the right. Follow the PCT northbound through timber on long switchbacks for roughly 5.5 to 6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk at about 5,400 ft, a narrow ledge blasted into the rock of Kendall Peak's south side — solid underfoot, very exposed, and worth care if icy or windy.

Continue north about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake at about 5,260 ft, the last reliable water and a common camp; roughly two to two and a half hours and about seven miles from the car.

About 0.4 to 0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching LEFT (west) off the PCT. It climbs a steep 200 ft to Bumblebee Pass at about 5,400 ft, above Alaska Lake. Drop off the far side into Bumblebee Basin, then contour and climb northwest across talus and scree toward the ridge.

About 8 to 8.5 miles and 2,900 to 3,000 ft to the base, typically four to five hours for a fit party.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AIM FOR THE LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE, AND KNOW IN ADVANCE THAT IT IS FURTHER LEFT THAN IT LOOKS. From Bumblebee Basin, scrambling up scree, the beginning of the ridge that you can see from below is NOT where you want to be. The notch you want is LEFT of it, at the ridge's lowest point, around 5,960 ft. That single correction is the most useful thing on this approach, because the eye pulls you right every time.

THE NOTCH IS SMALL, AND ITS SIZE IS THE CONFIRMATION: it holds about three people at most. If you have topped out on a broad, comfortable saddle, you are not at the start of the West Ridge.

EXPECT SHORT FOURTH-CLASS SCRAMBLING AROUND GENDARMES to reach it. Once you top out on the ridge you scramble over a small gendarme, traversing rightward toward the crest, to gain the notch itself.

THE FIRST MOVE SETTLES IT ABSOLUTELY: pitch one begins with a STEP LEFT INTO A WELL-FEATURED CHIMNEY. That step-left-into-a-chimney is the signature of this route and is probably the crux of the whole climb. If your first pitch is a face or a slab, you are not in the right notch. The first two leads run up a series of chimneys in solid rock.

AND THE OTHER ROUTE ON THIS PEAK IS ON THE OPPOSITE SIDE: the East Ridge is class 3-4 and is gained from a notch at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side, from the same basin. If you are on easy scrambling ground the whole way, you are on the East Ridge and you have circled to the wrong end of the mountain.
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk, exposed and dangerous when icy or windy
Loose and eroded tread on both sides of the Bumblebee Pass boot path
Talus and scree in the basin below the ridge
A descent by the East Ridge, meaning a route-finding descent on unfamiliar ground at the end of a long day
A long day: many parties climb it car to car

approach_variants.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the south-face basin, then the heather-and-talus slope to the ESE notch
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead at I-90 exit 52, about 3,000 ft, follow the PCT north through Commonwealth Basin and up the Kendall Ridge switchbacks. At roughly 5.5 to 5.7 miles you cross the Kendall Katwalk, the exposed cut in the cliff band most parties use as a progress checkpoint.

Continue north past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, the last reliable water before the high basin, and on to the foot of Bumblebee Pass. A short, steep, unmaintained climbers' path with loose tread climbs to the 5,400 ft pass, then drops down the north side into the open basin directly below Mount Thomson's south face — the same basin West Ridge parties camp in.

Roughly six to seven miles one way with about 3,600 ft of cumulative gain, since the up-and-over at Bumblebee adds height beyond the net summit gain. Three to five hours car to basin, nine to eleven hours round trip is typical.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE BASIN, LOOK FOR THE STEEP HEATHER-AND-TALUS SLOPE THAT LEADS TO AN OBVIOUS NOTCH AT ABOUT 5,600 FT ON THE EAST-SOUTHEAST RIDGE. Heather and talus rather than clean rock is the signal you are on the correct slope; the West Ridge side is scree and gendarmes.

THE ALTITUDE IS THE DISCRIMINATOR BETWEEN THE PEAK'S TWO ROUTES, AND IT IS WORTH SETTING YOUR ALTIMETER FOR: this notch is at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side. The West Ridge notch is at about 5,960 ft on the other end of the mountain. Roughly 360 ft and a full traverse of the peak separate them.

WHAT FOLLOWS CONFIRMS IT: from the notch, scramble up and TRAVERSE LEFT along the ridge crest on mostly class 2-3 ground to the base of the final summit block. Easy scrambling with a leftward traverse is right for this route. Chimneys and fifth-class corners are the West Ridge.

AND THE ROUTE ENDS AT ONE SPECIFIC OBSTACLE, WHICH IS THE BEST CONFIRMATION OF ALL: a short, exposed 20 ft CLASS 4 STEP guarding the true summit. Most parties protect it with a rope or a handline. If you reached a summit without meeting that step, you are on a false one.

USEFUL CONTEXT: this is the easiest way up the peak and it is also the standard descent for West Ridge parties, so a party coming down at you is normal rather than a sign of a mistake.
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk when icy or windy
Loose tread on the unmaintained Bumblebee Pass path, awkward with a pack
Loose talus and minor route-finding on the slope to the notch
A short but exposed class 4 step at the summit, downclimbed or rappelled on the way back
A long day with an up-and-over on the return

approach_variants.name: PCT and Commonwealth Creek trail, then a heather traverse to the red gully
approach_variants.season: June to October, once the heather bands and rock are dry and snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT trailhead at I-90 exit 52, hike the Pacific Crest Trail north to the Commonwealth Creek trail junction, then follow that trail for about two miles until Red Mountain comes into view.

Leave the trail and traverse on heather across the base of the mountain. The trail will often carry you too far WEST before you notice the peak, so expect to traverse back over the ridge and possibly downslope to reach the start.

Most parties climb the whole thing unroped and rope up only if they want to.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROCK IS THE MARKER AND IT IS BRIGHT RED. You are looking for a low-angle gully or ramp of SOLID, BRIGHT RED rock at the base of the mountain — solid is the operative word, because it is the most solid rock on a peak otherwise famous for being fractured. The colour and the low angle together identify it; nothing else on this flank looks like it.

AND THE OVERSHOOT TEST IS THE ONE TO REMEMBER, BECAUSE IT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING: IF YOU REACH RED MOUNTAIN POND, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR. Popping out of the trees on the flank of Red commonly puts a party too far west; the pond tells you so unambiguously. Turn back east and traverse on heather until the red gully appears.

WHAT THE FIRST GROUND SHOULD FEEL LIKE: class 3, no gear required, two pitches of it. If you are pulling on anything hard from the ground you are not in the ramp.

WHERE IT LEADS, SO YOU CAN CHECK YOURSELF LATER: you pop over a small ridge into the MAIN GULLY below the summit. Keep going up that until the summit block above you turns steep and roofy. That roofy steepening is the signal to move LEFT onto the class 2 hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge — or, if you want it, to continue directly up the block at class 4 or low 5 with a rope.
hazards: Rockfall onto parties below where the route funnels through gullies
Loose rock typical of Red Mountain, though the south ramp is the most solid ground on the peak
A steep and roofy direct finish on the summit block that needs a rope
Route-finding on the traverse in, where the trail tends to carry you west past the start

approach_variants.name: PCT to Red Pass, then the climbers' path up to the saddle
approach_variants.season: Mid-summer into early autumn, once the Red Pass approach and the rock are dry
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT trailhead at exit 52, hike the PCT north about two miles to the Commonwealth Creek / Red Mountain Trail #1033 junction. Follow that trail, crossing Commonwealth Creek, roughly 1.7 miles further, passing Red Mountain on your right and Red Pond on your left, to the Red Mountain Saddle — Red Pass — at about 5,320 ft. The old PCT dropped from here toward Goldmyer Hot Springs.

From the saddle, follow a winding climbers' path up to the base of the route. Allow about two hours for the approach from the trailhead, more if there is snow.

This is a short technical add-on for parties already scrambling in the Red Pass and Commonwealth Basin area, not a day out on its own.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THREE OVERSIZED BOLTS ARE THE PROOF, AND THEY ARE THE REASON THIS ROUTE IS FINDABLE AT ALL. The pitch carries THREE fixed bolts, described by everyone who has climbed it as monstrous — large enough that they make the route-finding, in the words of the route's own page, non-adventurous. If you are on a 30 m pitch of broken rock with three big bolts in it, you are on this route. If you cannot see a bolt, you are on the ridge somewhere else.

WHAT THE PITCH IS: a very short 30 m lead, broken rock, past a SLAB SECTION and then a small section of more featured rock to the top. There are many variations and they are all easy. So the difficulty will not identify it; the hardware will.

HOW TO GET TO IT FROM THE SADDLE, AND THE ONE THING TO KEEP STRAIGHT: from Red Pass the climbers' path winds WEST and up. Passing Red Mountain on your right and Red Pond on your left on the way in is the confirmation you are approaching the pass from the correct side.

A NAMING WARNING THAT COULD SEND YOU TO ANOTHER MOUNTAIN, AND IT IS A REAL ONE: the published location text for this route refers to a saddle between Lundin and East Lundin peaks, while the approach it gives goes to Red Pass and then west, which is Red Mountain's ground rather than Lundin's. SummitPost separately carries TWO different pages called East Ridge on Red Mountain — one describing this saddle-to-summit line over two false summits, and one describing a ridge traverse from Point 5720 near the Kendall Katwalk, which its own author recommends nobody repeat. Three descriptions, one name. Fix the peak by the saddle and the three bolts, not by the route name.

IF YOU CONTINUE OVER THE FALSE SUMMITS toward the main peak, the sequence from the Red Mountain Saddle is: up the southeast side of the first false summit, a 30 ft class 3 gully down at its northwest end, right (north) to the big notch, 50 ft up slabs on the far side, a contour across the heathery northeast side of the second false summit, over that summit, then 100 ft of class 3 down a moderate gully to the final notch at about 5,840 ft below the main summit.
hazards: Loose, fractured red rock along this ridge system, more pronounced than on the south face
Short but real exposure on the summit block
Possible steep snow on the contour across the northeast side of the second false summit in early or late season
Aging fixed bolts of unknown provenance as the only in-situ protection

approach_variants.name: PCT and Commonwealth Creek trail to the cairn by the tarn, then the west-slope boot path
approach_variants.season: July to October. Snow lingers in Commonwealth Basin and on the upper slope into early-to-mid July, and the fractured rock is genuinely unsafe wet, so late July to September is the sweet spot
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass West, I-90 exit 52. Follow the rerouted PCT north roughly 2 to 2.5 miles of well-graded trail through old growth. At the signed junction, turn LEFT (west) onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, and follow it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek, the one reliable water on the approach — fill up there, because the scramble slopes above are dry.

An older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin trail leaves about 20 yards up from the parking lot and switchbacks directly into the basin, rejoining near the same split. It is shorter, harder to follow, and not recommended in poor visibility.

About 12.9 km round trip and 2,900 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TAKEOFF IS MARKED BY A CAIRN PLANTED IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PATH, AND THAT IS THE ARRIVAL TEST. As the trail levels out near a small tarn below Red Mountain's west slope, a cairn sits in the middle of the tread. That is where the scramble leaves the maintained trail. A cairn off to one side is not it; this one is in the way, deliberately.

FROM THE CAIRN, WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO: a boot path climbs the west slope. It is intermittent and easy to lose on scree. THE RULE WHEN YOU LOSE IT IS TO STAY CLOSE TO THE RIDGE CREST ON CLIMBERS' RIGHT — the south side. That single rule replaces route-finding for the whole upper slope, and it also keeps you off the loose gut of the scree where you would be kicking rock onto people.

WHAT THE LAST 900 FT SHOULD FEEL LIKE: a 30 to 40 degree slope of fractured, iron-stained RED rock, loose scree, heather and scattered alpine trees, alternating class 2 and low class 3, with no real exposure. Hands needed intermittently. If you are on genuinely exposed ground with real fall consequence, you have drifted off the line.

AND THE MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE, WHICH IS ABOUT THE DESCENT BUT BELONGS HERE: do NOT traverse east or south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Katwalk as a shortcut. That terrain becomes class 3 and 4 and cliffs out without a rope.

HONEST NOTE ON THE ROCK: helmets are for the whole party, not just a leader. Red Mountain's rock is notoriously fractured and there are documented close calls with softball- and grapefruit-sized rock near the summit.
hazards: Rockfall on loose, heavily fractured red rock, with documented close calls near the summit
Slick, dangerous rock when wet — an easy class 2 slope becomes unsafe in rain
Route-finding above the basin tarn where maintained trail becomes a cairned boot path
Lingering snow and postholing into early summer
Cliffed-out class 3-4 ground if a party tries to shortcut east toward the Kendall Katwalk

approach_variants.name: PCT north to the stump at 5,200 ft, then the boot path east
approach_variants.season: June to October; snow can linger in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse below Kendall Gardens into early summer
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 52 the PCT northbound lot sits just off the ramp on a short dirt spur; a Northwest Forest Pass is required and the roughly 50-car lot fills early at weekends.

From about 3,000 ft, follow the PCT north through second growth: first switchback at 0.6 mile, a switchback pair at 1.5 miles, the wilderness boundary at 2.0 miles where the forest opens into talus. The trail eases slightly downhill to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction at 2.6 miles — stay RIGHT and straight on the PCT; the left-hand Commonwealth Basin trail is brushy and easy to mistake for the main tread. Two stream crossings near that junction are the last reliable water.

Beyond, the PCT climbs under Kendall Peak's west flank through open talus and heather — Kendall Gardens, around mile 5 — then switchbacks directly below the peak at about 5.5 to 6 miles and 5,100 to 5,200 ft.

About 7.4 km and 2,800 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MARKER IS A STUMP, AND IT IS IN YOUR WAY. At about 5,200 ft on the switchbacks below the peak, a large, distinctive stump partially blocks the LEFT side of the trail. Roughly 15 FEET BEYOND IT a boot path forks RIGHT (east) and climbs straight uphill. That stump-then-fifteen-feet pairing is the whole finding, and it works in cloud because you feel the stump on the trail rather than having to spot the peak.

WHAT FOLLOWS CONFIRMS IT: the final 400 to 500 vertical feet on that boot path are steep, loose dirt and scree with occasional hands-on class 2 moves, running to the NORTHERNMOST and highest summit. Steep loose dirt is right; if you are on rock and using your hands continuously, you are somewhere harder.

THE OVERSHOOT AND WHAT IT COSTS YOU, WHICH IS THE REASON TO CARE ABOUT THE STUMP: parties who miss it and carry on along the PCT to where it crosses the ridge on the east side can scramble the ridge crest south to the true summit instead. That line is class 3 to 4, has abundant loose rock, and is notably more exposed and dangerous. It is a real alternative, but it is not the standard route and you should choose it deliberately rather than by accident.

AND THE PROGRESS CHECK BEFORE THE STUMP: Kendall Gardens, the open talus and heather at about mile 5, is the last obvious landmark below the switchbacks. If you have crossed the Kendall Katwalk you have gone a long way past the turn.
hazards: Steep, loose dirt and scree on the final boot path
Lingering snow in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse into early summer
The class 3-4 ridge alternative, more exposed and loose than the standard route, entered by accident if the stump is missed
No water above the Commonwealth Creek crossings
