approach_variants.name: PCT then the old Commonwealth Creek trail, stopping short of the creek
approach_variants.season: Winter into early spring, when the two ice pitches have formed. Assess the avalanche slide path between the pitches before committing
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, follow the PCT and, at an early fork, break LEFT onto the old, overgrown Commonwealth Creek trail. Follow it until the trees open out into a clearing where the cliff and its ice come into view.

This is a short approach on trail or on whatever bootpack exists. There is no fixed hardware on the climb — descent is two rappels off ice-screw or V-thread anchors from cord and slings you carry in.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE STOP SIGNAL IS A CREEK YOU MUST NOT CROSS. Follow the old Commonwealth Creek trail until the timber opens into a clearing with the cliff and the ice in front of you. DO NOT CROSS COMMONWEALTH CREEK. If you have crossed it, you have gone too far and the cliff is behind you. That is the cleanest fog test on this side of the pass, because a creek crossing is unmistakable underfoot even when you cannot see a cliff.

THE CLEARING IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE TEST: you are looking for the point where the trees end, not for a distance or a time. Overgrown trail, then open ground, then the ice. If you are still under timber you have not arrived.

WHAT THE CLIMB SHOULD BE, AS CONFIRMATION: two pitches. Pitch one is the harder, sustained and near-vertical. Pitch two eases off and is belayed from a SMALL CAVE that offers some shelter. A cave belay at the top of the second pitch is the confirming feature.

AND THE HAZARD THAT SITS INSIDE THE FINDING: there can be a snow slide path between the two pitches. Assess it before you commit to the first pitch, not from the belay above it.
hazards: A slide path for snow between the two pitches — assess avalanche conditions before committing
No fixed anchors: descent is on ice screws or V-threads with cord you carry
A sustained, near-vertical first pitch on winter ice of variable formation
A north-facing cliff that stays cold and holds thin ice in lean winters

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake, Rampart Ridge, and the boulder gully to the 5,570 ft saddle
approach_variants.season: July to October. The route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Rachel Lake trailhead at 2,800 ft, at the end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Road from I-90 exit 62, take Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first 2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek at a gentle grade with reliable water throughout.

At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses the creek and hits the section known locally as the mile from hell: a heavily rooted, rocky climb gaining roughly 1,300 ft in a mile with big step-ups and no switchbacks. It is the fitness crux of the day, not a technical one.

At Rachel Lake, 4,700 ft, a use trail branches right near the outhouse, skirts the lake's north side, and switchbacks steeply about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest at about 5,100 ft. At the ridge junction go LEFT (south) for Rampart Lakes, and follow the ridge and the east side of the lakes basin. Stay on maintained tread through the basin; the alpine turf is fragile and shortcut social trails are often deliberately blocked.

About 6 to 6.5 miles and 3,000 ft to the saddle.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT THE SOUTH END OF THE RAMPART LAKES, FIND A LARGE BOULDER GULLY WITH CLIFF BANDS ON ITS LEFT — THAT IS, ITS WEST — SIDE. Boulders in the gully, cliffs bounding it on the west: that pairing is the arrival test for the scramble takeoff, and it does not require seeing Alta.

WHERE IT PUTS YOU: a boot path up that gully reaches a broad saddle at about 5,570 ft on the Rampart Ridge crest. Broad saddle at 5,570 ft is your altimeter confirmation. From there the route turns WEST along the crest toward Alta's summit block.

WHAT THE RIDGE THEN DOES, SO YOU CAN COUNT YOUR WAY ALONG IT: THREE FALSE SUMMITS, class 2-3 rock steps, at least one near-vertical step of 6 to 8 ft with good holds and serious exposure, and a class 3 DOWNCLIMB crux near the top. A party that has crossed one bump and thinks it is at the summit is two bumps early.

AND THE ONE PLACE WHERE THE FINDING IS A WARNING RATHER THAN A DIRECTION: there is a section where the path skirts a cliff edge. Fall consequences there are serious. This route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge, and it is not a place for anyone uneasy with heights or for dogs.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT DESCRIPTION OF THE SAME TAKEOFF: an unsigned climbers' path marked by a CAIRN leaves the maintained trail near the Rachel Lake / Lila Lake junction and climbs the south ridge. Steep, loose, big steps and no shade at first, then it moderates onto the knife-edge crest.
hazards: Sustained exposure along the ridge crest, including a section skirting a cliff edge
Three false summits and a class 3 downclimb crux near the top
Loose rock and large step-ups on the initial climbers' path
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long exposed crest
Lingering snow in the approach gully in early season

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake Trail to the avalanche clearing, then the Hibox climbers' path over two cliff bands
approach_variants.season: July to October
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rachel Lake trailhead, Trail #1313, about 2,800 ft, at the end of Box Canyon Road / FR-4930. The trail climbs gently through forest along Box Canyon Creek, easy class 1 walking.

At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles and about 3,300 ft the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing. That clearing is the key landmark, because Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast from it.

Above the boot path the tread climbs steeply, mostly class 2 with fallen timber, about 500 vertical feet to a band of cliffs near 5,300 ft. Stay RIGHT of that first band, then work LEFT around a rock outcrop, continue through patchy timber to a SECOND, higher cliff band, and take the gully on the RIGHT through it. Above, a large sloping subalpine meadow funnels into loose talus and scree.

No reliable water past the lower forest. About 8 km and 3,900 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLEARING IS THE FIRST TEST AND THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS ITS PROOF. At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles the maintained trail crosses a brushy avalanche clearing, and from it Hibox's summit block is visible on the ridge to the NORTHEAST. Just past that clearing — some parties say after the SECOND such clearing — watch the RIGHT, climbers'-right, side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path heading northeast and uphill into the forest. It is easy to walk past if you are not looking.

THE TWO CLIFF BANDS ARE A COUNTED SEQUENCE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT IN FOG: first band, pass it on the RIGHT; then LEFT around a rock outcrop; second band, take the gully on the RIGHT. Two bands, right then left then right. If you have passed only one band you are not yet on the upper mountain.

AND HERE IS THE WRONG-TURN TRAP THAT MATTERS MOST, at the top: the talus tops out on the SOUTH side of the summit block, and the rock straight above you there is steeper and more broken than it looks. That is the spot where parties commit to the wrong line, and there is a deceptive gully on the SOUTHWEST side of the block that cliffs out at class 4. Do not climb what is above you.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL BASE FINDING: work RIGHT, staying along the south side of the rock and heading EAST, on loose talus over a sloping bed, until a reasonable gully opens on the EAST side of the block. That east gully is the route. It stays easy until the top, where a short NOTCH or narrow chimney gives a bit of genuine class 3 on good, solid holds to a small summit platform.

AND A DESCENT NOTE THAT BELONGS WITH THE FINDING: the boot path through the brushy avalanche clearings is easy to lose on the way down, especially in fog. Look back at the junction on the way up.
hazards: An unsigned, easy-to-lose boot path through brushy avalanche clearings, especially confusing in fog and on descent
A deceptive gully on the southwest side of the summit block that cliffs out at class 4 — stay climbers' right of it
Loose talus and scree above about 4,600 ft with real rockfall risk onto parties below
An exposed class 3 notch and chimney on the summit block, whose downclimb is the part to think about before committing
Lingering snow and ice in the upper gully and basin into early summer

approach_variants.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile SHORT of Chikamin Pass
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the 5,200 ft pack camp and make it a two or three day trip.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS TO LEAVE THE TRAIL BEFORE YOU REACH THE PASS, AND THAT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE ENOUGH THAT IT IS THE WHOLE FINDING. At roughly mile 13.5 — about HALF A MILE SHORT of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp at about 5,200 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy and heather slopes into the gully systems on the south and southeast face.

THE NEGATIVE IS EXPLICIT AND EXPENSIVE: do NOT continue to Chikamin Pass before cutting uphill. Doing so puts you in the middle of the FOUR BROTHERS, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain on a route that is otherwise a scramble. If you are standing at Chikamin Pass, you have overshot the turn.

SO USE THE PACK CAMP AS THE MARKER: an established camp at about 5,200 ft on the trail, with the peak's south face above and the pass still ahead of you. Turn uphill there.

WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO, IN ORDER: class 2 hiking low on grass and heather, then loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 as you gain Chikamin Ridge with some exposure near the crest, and finally a short, well-protected class 3-4 CHIMNEY or slot of about 10 ft right below the summit block, with roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling above it to the top. A 10 ft chimney immediately below the summit horn is the confirming feature.

SNOW CHANGES THE CHARACTER OF THE GULLY ENTIRELY: early in the season it is a steep, rubble-choked chute and an axe is needed.
hazards: An unmarked gully turnoff near Chikamin Pass — overshooting puts you in the cliffy Four Brothers
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gully system
A steep, snow-filled and rubble-choked gully in early season
Short but exposed class 3 moves on the summit horn
A long trail approach with camps well short of the peak

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THIS SIDE THE ARRIVAL IS A LAKE, NOT A TRAIL JUNCTION: you climb the gullies directly ABOVE GLACIER LAKE. Standing at the lake with the southeast slopes rising in front of you is the arrival, and the lake is a hard landmark that cloud does not remove.

WHAT THE GROUND BELOW THE GULLIES LOOKS LIKE, AS CONFIRMATION: brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down. Running water and heather benches are right for this side; if you are on bare scree from the lake upward, you have started too high.

THE TWO APPROACHES MEET ON THE SAME UPPER MOUNTAIN, so the finding from there is identical: loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 to the crest of Chikamin Ridge, and a short well-protected 10 ft class 3-4 chimney below the summit block with about 75 ft of easy scrambling above it.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE APPLIES ONCE YOU ARE ON THE PCT: do not wander south toward Chikamin Pass looking for a way up. The Four Brothers sit between the pass and the route.
hazards: Brushy lower trail and creek crossings on the Mineral Creek approach
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gullies
Exposure near the final ridge crest

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT to the Lemah Creek climbers' path, then the col below the Main Peak
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 80 at Roslyn / Salmon la Sac, drive SR-903 north 16.8 miles through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake, then west on FR-46 for 4.7 miles and right on FR-4616 for a mile to the Cooper Lake / Pete Lake trailhead.

Follow Pete Lake Trail #1323 along the Cooper River about 4.5 miles to Pete Lake, continue past it and pick up the PCT southbound for roughly four more miles to the Lemah Creek crossing, then follow the PCT south under a mile.

A faint, unmaintained climbers' trail leaves on the NORTH side of Lemah Creek, marked by occasional flagging, with deadfall and brush for the first 400 vertical feet. It passes waterfalls and swimming holes and reaches a meadow at about 3,600 ft where the creek breaks into shallow ponds — the common camp. A thick band of slide alder guards the far end of that meadow and is best bypassed through the timber to the north.

About 12.9 km and 4,480 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL YOU ARE AIMING FOR IS A COL, AND IT IS THE COL BETWEEN LEMAH TWO AND THE MAIN PEAK. From the 3,600 ft meadow camp, follow the drainage to about 5,000 ft where the Lemah Glacier remnant begins, climb to roughly 6,200 ft, then exit SOUTH — climbers' left — up a short cliff onto glacial remnants on the peak's southeast side, and traverse northwest to the base of that col. Everything technical on this route starts from the col; below it you are walking, scrambling class 2-3 cliff bands, and crossing snow.

THE CONFIRMING FEATURE ABOVE THE COL IS A CHUTE, AND ITS CHARACTER IS DISTINCTIVE: a snow slope and then a chute of mixed steep snow or ice and class 3-4 rock, OFTEN WITH WATER RUNNING DOWN IT. Running water in the chute is the signature of this line and is why parties carry crampons and an axe even in summer. That chute is the technical crux of the route.

THE ALTITUDE SEQUENCE IS THE FOG TEST: 3,600 ft camp, 5,000 ft glacier remnant, 6,200 ft, then exit left up a short cliff. Four altimeter checks and one turn, none of which needs the summit to be visible.

AND THE NEGATIVE: if you are climbing toward a summit without having stood in a col between two distinct peaks, you are on the wrong feature. Lemah Two is the second of the Lemah summits and the Main Peak — Lemah Three — is the one across the col from you.

PLAN THE DOWNCLIMB BEFORE YOU COMMIT TO THE CHUTE. Summit day here is long and parties frequently finish the descent to camp after dark.
hazards: A faint, unmaintained climbers' trail with deadfall and brush for the first 400 vertical feet
A thick band of slide alder at the far end of the meadow camp

A moat where the glacier remnant meets the rock

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek Trail, then off-trail through the vine maple to the south-side talus
approach_variants.season: June to September
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead at about 2,400 ft, cross the Kachess River ford, follow 1.7 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek crossing, then about a mile further through vine maple brush to the base of the long talus slope on Middle Peak's south side.

This shares the trailhead and initial trail with the East / Main Peak standard route, and the divergence is where you leave the trail into the brush.

About 4.3 km beyond the road and 4,600 ft of gain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH YOU WANT IS MARKED BY A CHOCKSTONE, AND THAT IS THE ONE UNAMBIGUOUS OBJECT ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. The long south-side talus steepens toward the notch between the MAIN and MIDDLE peaks, and a chockstone sits in that notch. Chockstone in the gap between two summits: that is your arrival, and it is a thing rather than a description.

FROM THE NOTCH THE LINE IS A LEDGE, NOT A RIDGE. Traverse a BROAD SOUTH-FACING LEDGE to a rock gable roughly 150 ft below the summit. If you are on a crest rather than on a wide ledge, you have taken the ridge instead of the traverse.

AND THE CLIMBING ITSELF CONFIRMS IT: a solid, enjoyable CLASS 4 CHIMNEY runs directly from the gable to the top. Solid rock is worth noting because so little on this peak is. If the ground above the gable is loose scrambling rather than a defined chimney, you are not at the gable.

THE DESCENT IS THE MIRROR AND IT IS SHORT: two 60 ft rappels down the South Chimney regain the ledge system, then reverse the talus and the trail.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER LINES: the standard scramble goes to the East / Main Peak and the West Peak is reached from Spectacle Point on a multi-day approach. If you have walked past the Main-Middle notch and are heading for a different summit, you are on a different route.
hazards: An unbridged Kachess River ford at the trailhead
Off-trail travel through vine maple brush to reach the talus
Long loose talus below the notch
A class 4 chimney and a broad exposed ledge traverse
Rockfall onto anyone in the notch below the chimney

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek Trail to the break in the timber west of the waterfall gully
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at roughly 2,360 to 2,400 ft via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass, the trail promptly crosses the Kachess River — look for logs, and wade if they are not there. It climbs gently north through second growth and brushy old avalanche paths, muddy in places with occasional blowdown.

At about 1.6 to 1.7 miles it crosses Mineral Creek itself, which carries enough current in early season that parties often lay a log rather than ford. The ruins of an old mine and mill sit just off-trail here — a landmark and the last good water.

Continue upstream through brushy trail roughly another mile, to about the 2.7-mile mark.

About 8.85 km, with 1,400 to 1,700 ft of off-trail gain above the trail.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TAKEOFF IS A BREAK IN THE TIMBER ON THE RIGHT, AND THE WAY TO GET IT RIGHT IS TO KNOW WHICH DRAINAGE IT IS NOT. At about 2.7 miles, between roughly 3,300 and 3,500 ft, watch on the RIGHT (west) for a break in the timber where an obvious boot and social path leaves the maintained trail and cuts west through 100 to 200 ft of vine maple brush to the base of the south-face talus.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: leave the trail WEST OF THE BROAD WATERFALL GULLY that drains the south face — NOT at the drainage directly above the Mineral Creek crossing. Trip reports flag exactly this junction as easy to get wrong in the brush, and the two drainages are the reason. Old mine ruins at the creek crossing, then roughly another mile, then the break past the waterfall gully.

WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO ONCE YOU ARE OFF TRAIL, in order, so you can check yourself without seeing the peak: the lower 1,000 ft is moderately angled, largely stable LARGE talus. Above that the rock turns smaller and looser and funnels into choss gullies, class 2 with short class 3 steps. A snow ramp is commonly met around 5,200 ft and can persist into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season.

THE FINAL 400 FT IS THE MOST EXPOSED GROUND ON THE ROUTE, with brief but genuine class 3 and blocks that shift underfoot. Guidebook descriptions calling this section class 3 are considered generous by parties who found it heads-up throughout.

A CONFLICT IN THE RECORD, STATED RATHER THAN RESOLVED: this row also carries a description of an approach from a camp at Upper or Middle Park Lake, ascending to the Main-Middle notch and traversing onto a broad LEDGE SYSTEM ON THE NORTH FACE for the last 200 ft, because the crest directly above the notch degenerates into class 5. That is a different side of the mountain from the Mineral Creek south-talus line above. Both are documented; decide which you are climbing before you leave the car, and do not expect the markers from one to appear on the other.
hazards: An unbridged Kachess River crossing at the trailhead and a Mineral Creek crossing with real current in early season
A brushy, easy-to-miss trail departure between two similar drainages
Loose rock and rockfall through the upper talus and choss gullies — helmets, and keep the group tight
A snow ramp around 5,200 ft persisting into midsummer
Brief but genuine class 3 with shifting blocks on the final 400 ft, harder than the guidebook grade suggests

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and the PCT, then the Shovel Creek fisherman's trail to the foot of the slab
approach_variants.season: July to September; documented ascents cluster in August
approach_variants.notes:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, hike the Waptus River Trail about nine miles to Waptus Lake. The bridge has been out, so wade or rock-hop the river at the horse ford. Where the trail joins the PCT, head SOUTHBOUND (west).

Shortly before the PCT crosses the Waptus River, leave the trail and head northwest toward a faint shoulder and bench through flat, easy forest. Pick up a fisherman's trail on the southwest side of that bench and follow it toward Shovel Creek, then up and over the bench past an informal campsite with a GIANT CAIRN, where it starts to climb the shoulder on the EAST side of Shovel Creek.

Before long the trail leaves the forest straight onto talus. Easy talus walking brings you to Shovel Creek; cross where convenient.

Roughly 13 miles to the base, five to six hours. Most parties camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CROSSING SHOVEL CREEK OFF THE TALUS PUTS YOU AT THE FOOT OF THE MEGA SLAB — THAT IS THE ARRIVAL, AND IT IS A CREEK CROSSING RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT. The slab drops from the peak's southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft all the way to Shovel Creek at about 3,700 ft, so there is no ambiguity about which piece of rock it is: it is the enormous unbroken sheet above you, one of the longest continuous sandstone slabs in North America.

WHICH LINE ON THE SLAB IS THE REAL QUESTION HERE, AND FOR THIS ROUTE THE ANSWER IS A SINGLE WORD: LOWEST. Infinite Beauty begins at the LOWEST PART of the slab, on a SHALLOW RIB. Walk the base downhill until it stops going down, and start on the rib there.

HOW THAT DISTINGUISHES IT FROM ITS NEIGHBOUR: Timeless Treasure climbs the MIDDLE of the slab. So if you have walked out along the base looking for a nicer-looking start, you are on Timeless Treasure. The lowest point is the whole distinction and it is decidable by walking downhill rather than by looking.

WHAT THE ROCK SHOULD FEEL LIKE, AS CONFIRMATION: clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone with minimal breaks, and roughly 2,000 ft of sustained fourth class. Approach shoes or trail runners friction well on it and most of the slab is climbed unroped. If you are pulling into cracks or dodging vegetation, you are off the clean sheet.

AND WHERE THE ROUTE ENDS ITS OWN IDENTITY: after about 2,000 ft the line naturally angles RIGHT and joins Timeless Treasure for brief, unexposed low-fifth moves up overlaps trending up and right to the southeast shoulder. Easy scrambling then leads to the summit block, where the rock quality noticeably deteriorates over the final three pitches.
hazards: About 2,000 ft of unprotected friction slab, mostly climbed unroped
Rock quality deteriorating markedly on the final three summit-block pitches
No water on the slab — carry the whole climbing day's supply
A long, remote approach with no confirmed cell coverage
The Shovel Lake descent alternative involves loose dirt high, brush and cliff bands low, and heavy route-finding

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and the PCT, then the Shovel Creek track to the middle of the slab
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, follow the Waptus River Trail and the PCT roughly twelve flat miles to Waptus Lake and a camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge. The Waptus River bridge has been out, so plan on a ford at the horse crossing.

From camp, an old, faint, unmaintained track parallels Shovel Creek through forest to a bench around 3,400 ft, then talus-hops to the base of the Mega Slab at roughly 3,700 ft.

About 19.3 km one way and 4,697 ft of gain.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
SAME SLAB, DIFFERENT PLACE ON IT: THIS ROUTE TAKES THE MIDDLE. Once you have crossed Shovel Creek off the talus and are standing under the Mega Slab, walk along the base to its MIDDLE and start there. The slab runs from about 3,700 ft at the creek to the southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft, so the middle is a real and findable place along a very long base.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST ITS NEIGHBOUR IS A SINGLE STEP: Infinite Beauty starts at the LOWEST point of the slab, on a shallow rib. If you are at the bottom end of the base, you are on Infinite Beauty. Walk up along the base until you are in the middle of the sheet.

WHAT THE ROCK SHOULD FEEL LIKE: perfect stone, mostly fourth class with occasional low-fifth moves higher up. If it is broken or vegetated you have drifted off the clean centre of the slab.

WHERE THE TWO ROUTES MERGE, AND WHY THAT MATTERS TO THE FINDING: both finish on the SAME three-pitch 5.6+ summit block. So being on the correct route matters for the first 2,000 ft and stops mattering above the shoulder. If you are already on the summit block and unsure which line you climbed, the question no longer has a practical answer.

A PRACTICAL NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE FINDING HERE: most parties either reverse the slab, which is easy and secure, or descend toward Shovel Lake. Reversing is the recommended option precisely because you already know that ground.
hazards: A long, remote approach with no confirmed reliable cell coverage
Loose rock and heavy route-finding on the Shovel Lake descent
No water on the slab itself
Deteriorating rock on the shared summit-block pitches

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie and Williams Creek to Dutch Miller Gap, then a camp below the face
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
From North Bend, take I-90 to exit 34, follow 468th Ave SE north 0.6 mile, then right onto Middle Fork Road, FS Road 56. Continue twelve miles as the pavement gives out and roughens, then about five more rough miles — high clearance recommended — to the Dutch Miller Gap trailhead at the old roadbed terminus, about 2,850 ft.

Hike the Middle Fork Snoqualmie / Williams Creek corridor roughly fifteen miles to Dutch Miller Gap, about four and three quarter hours, then continue to a camp below the southwest face. The whole outing is about 22 miles of trail.

Camp to summit runs about six hours and summit to camp about four and three quarter, so budget a full day above camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE COUNTING GULLIES, AND THERE ARE EXACTLY TWO. The southwest face carries TWO PARALLEL GULLIES. Take the LEFT-HAND one. That is the entire base finding and it works in cloud because two parallel features are countable from close range without seeing the summit.

WHAT THE LEFT GULLY SHOULD DELIVER: roughly 1,000 ft of class 3-4 ground ending at a RIDGE NOTCH NORTHWEST of the true summit. Notch on the ridge, summit up and to your southeast: that is the correct arrival at the technical climbing.

THE ROPED PART IS SHORT AND ITS SHAPE CONFIRMS THE LINE: three short pitches to 5.6 up the summit block from that notch. Not a long face climb — three pitches. If you are looking at hundreds of feet of steep rock above the notch, you are at the wrong notch.

AND THE DESCENT MIRRORS IT EXACTLY, which is worth knowing before you start up: three single-rope rappels down the WEST side of the summit block back to the notch, then downclimb the class 3-4 gully. A 50 m rope suffices; a 60 m or two 50 m ropes is better for a party of three. Route-finding through the ledges on the way down is reported as the crux of the descent and slower than the ascent.

HISTORICAL CONFIRMATION THAT THIS IS THE ORDINARY WAY UP THE PEAK: this face gave the mountain's first ascent, on 8 August 1939, by Fred Beckey at sixteen with Joe Barto and Wayne Swift.
hazards: Loose, broken rock throughout the gully and the lower pitches
Marginal protection near an old, deteriorating piton at the pitch 1 crux
Complex, slow route-finding through ledges on the descent
A long, remote multi-day approach on a rough forest road with limited rescue access
No walk-off once on the roped summit block: the three rappels are the only reasonable retreat

approach_variants.name: The gated Middle Fork road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Dingford Creek trailhead gate and walk — or mountain-bike, which is the sensible choice — the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about seven miles.

The boot path for the Hardscrabble Lakes leaves roughly half a mile SHORT of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a LARGE FALLEN LOG. Follow the climbers' path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake.

About 20 km and 5,300 ft, and very light foot traffic — do not expect a reliable boot path throughout.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAIL DEPARTURE IS MARKED BY A FALLEN LOG ACROSS THE ROAD FROM IT, AND IT IS HALF A MILE SHORT OF THE HORSE CAMP. Those two facts together are what make it findable, because the boot path itself is unmarked. If you have reached the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, you have gone about half a mile too far.

THE RULE THAT KEEPS YOU ALIVE ON THE WAY TO THE LAKES: climbing past the lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, STAY CLOSE TO THE INLET. Straying LEFT leads into cliff bands, and the east face and buttress above the lower lake drop directly into the water in steep walls. Inlet on your side, cliffs away to the left.

FROM UPPER HARDSCRABBLE LAKE, THE SEQUENCE IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: climb a gully to a COL, drop onto the OPEN GRANITE SLAB of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit. Gully, col, granite slab, ridge. If you top the gully and are not looking at an open slab of granite, you are at the wrong col.

WHAT THIS ROUTE IS NOT: the East BUTTRESS is a ten-pitch technical line on the same side of the mountain, reached from the LOWER lake rather than the upper one. If you are roping up, you are on the buttress and not on this route.
hazards: The east face and buttress above lower Hardscrabble Lake are steep and cliffy — stay on the inlet-side path
A long, remote approach with no maintained trail for the final stretch
Very light foot traffic, so no dependable boot path
Early-season snow in the gully to the col
A multi-mile road walk out at the end of a long day

approach_variants.name: As for the East Ridge, but stopping at the LOWER Hardscrabble Lake
approach_variants.season: July to September
approach_variants.notes:
Approach exactly as for the East Ridge / Hardscrabble route: walk or bike the gated Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path — half a mile short of the old horse camp, across the road from a large fallen log — and follow the climbers' path east through forest.

The difference is that this route stops at the LOWER lake rather than continuing to the upper one.

This line sees very few repeat ascents, so beta is thin and any fixed anchors should be treated as unreliable.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LAKE TELLS YOU WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ON: this one belongs to the LOWER Hardscrabble Lake, and the East Ridge belongs to the upper one. If you have walked on to the upper lake, you have passed the buttress.

FROM THE LOWER LAKE THE SEQUENCE IS COUNTED, AND THE COUNT IS TWO: traverse the lake's LEFT — north — side, then scramble over TWO ROCK BANDS to reach the SOUTH side of the buttress at about 5,400 ft. Two bands and an altimeter reading of 5,400 ft is the arrival test. One band means you are not there yet.

THE FEATURE ITSELF IS UNMISTAKABLE ONCE YOU ARE UNDER IT: the east face and buttress drop directly into the lower lake in steep walls. A buttress rising straight out of the water below you and a south flank you have just scrambled onto is the correct position.

WHAT THE CLIMBING SHOULD BE: ten pitches close to the crest, working under overhangs, on generally SOLID GRANITE — originally four pitches of class 4 followed by class 5 with occasional aid pitons, later freed at about 5.10. Solid granite close to a crest, with overhangs to work beneath, is the confirmation. Loose scrambling means you are on the ridge route instead.

HONEST LIMIT, STATED BECAUSE IT MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL HERE: this is a thin record. The published position is the lake side, the two bands and the 5,400 ft elevation, and that is all. Nothing finer is documented, and the route sees so few ascents that no worn line will help you.
hazards: The east face and buttress drop directly into lower Hardscrabble Lake in steep walls
Very few repeat ascents, so beta and any fixed anchors may be sparse or unreliable
The original ascent used aid pitons on the class 5 sections; free beta is secondhand
A long, remote approach with a road walk or bike out
No documented descent line for the buttress itself

approach_variants.name: Dingford Creek Trail to Myrtle Lake, then off-trail past Big Snow and Snowflake Lakes
approach_variants.season: July to September, best once the gullies and couloir have melted out
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Dingford Creek trailhead gate via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road / FSR 56, about eighteen miles from North Bend, with the last several miles rough gravel and high clearance recommended.

Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 miles to the Hester Lake Trail junction, then continue LEFT (east) toward Myrtle Lake, about two miles more.

From Myrtle Lake the maintained trail ends. Serious route-finding and bushwhacking start here and failed attempts from losing the line are common.

About 9.7 km and 5,280 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THREE LAKES IN ORDER ARE THE WHOLE NAVIGATION, AND THEY ARE THE ONLY THINGS ON THIS ROUTE THAT CLOUD CANNOT TAKE AWAY: MYRTLE, then BIG SNOW, then SNOWFLAKE. Leave the maintained trail at Myrtle Lake. Climb steep, increasingly brushy ground to Big Snow Lake. Then traverse RIGHT around Snowflake Lake. If you have not passed a lake in the last while, you are off the line.

WHERE THE CLIMBING BEGINS: above Snowflake Lake, ascend gullies and chutes — a snow couloir early in the season — on the mountain's northwest flank to the upper rock fields. The transition from brush and heather to rock fields is the arrival at the climbing proper, and it is a change underfoot rather than a view.

WHAT THE FINAL GROUND IS: class 2-3 scrambling across the upper rock fields to the summit. If you find yourself needing a rope, you have wandered into steeper ground than this route takes.

THE HONEST WARNING, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE HERE: there is no maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake and light foot traffic keeps any boot path faint. Parties fail on this peak by losing the line rather than by finding the climbing hard. Carry a track, and treat the lake sequence as the route.
hazards: No maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake, and any boot path stays faint
Steep gullies and chutes above Big Snow Lake holding snow or ice well into summer
Crumbly, mossy rock in the chutes
Remote, seldom-visited terrain with real self-rescue implications
Rough gravel road access with high clearance recommended

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley in spring, river braids and a camp below the face
approach_variants.season: A narrow spring window, roughly March to April, while the ice and snowfields are in. This line forms only briefly and has almost no repeat trip-report history
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road, NF-56, to its plowed or drivable end, then bike or hike the remaining distance — about a mile in the first-ascent party's case — into the valley.

Continue on foot through snowy forest along the valley trail, crossing MULTIPLE BRAIDS of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie. Those crossings are the crux of the approach in high water and are unprotected. Then climb to a camp below the north face. The first-ascent party took about six and a half hours from vehicle to camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST AND MOST IMPORTANT FINDING IS WHETHER THERE IS ANYTHING TO FIND. This face is condition-only. The single published account is the first ascent, and it describes roughly 2,000 vertical feet linking runnels and couloirs, with the defining section being a RAMP HOLDING ABOUT 600 VERTICAL FEET OF WATER ICE at WI2 to WI3. If that ramp is not iced, there is no route at the base and no amount of searching will produce one. Look for the ramp from the valley before committing to the walk in.

THE ARRIVAL ITSELF IS A CAMP, NOT A NOTCH: you are aiming for camp below the face, and the base of the climb is the lowest runnel beneath the ice ramp. There is no published discriminating feature at ground level beyond the ramp, and this entry does not invent one.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE, SO YOU CAN CHECK YOURSELF ONCE COMMITTED: about 600 ft of WI2-3 water ice on the ramp, then a first snowfield, then a second snowfield, then an AI2 exit step near the summit. Two distinct snowfields separated by easier ground is the confirmation you are on the line the first ascent took.

A PROTECTION WARNING THAT BELONGS WITH THE FINDING BECAUSE IT COMES FROM THE ONLY PARTY WHO HAS BEEN THERE: they carried only two titanium ice screws and found that badly short for the ice actually encountered, supplementing with knifeblade pitons in compact rock between ice sections. Rock protection on the ice section is scarce. Carry a real screw rack.

AND PLAN THE DESCENT BEFORE YOU START, BECAUSE RETREAT FROM HIGH ON THE FACE IS NOT SIMPLE: the first ascent did not reverse the route. They descended the SOUTHWEST side, downclimbing neve and making two 30 m rappels down a snow gully to a col west of the peak.

READ EVERYTHING ABOVE AS ONE PARTY'S CONDITIONS, NOT AS AN ANNUAL EXPECTATION.
hazards: A rarely-climbed alpine ice route with essentially no repeat beta
Difficult, unprotected crossings of multiple river braids on the approach
Avalanche and wet-slide hazard on the spring approach and the snowfields

A descent by an unfamiliar side of the peak at the end of a committing route

approach_variants.name: PCT past the Kendall Katwalk to a point due EAST of the summit, then straight up
approach_variants.season: July to October
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft, hike the PCT northbound past Kendall Pass and the Kendall Katwalk to Ridge Lake, then past Alaska Pass and around Alaska Mountain to Huckleberry Flats. The Commonwealth Basin shortcut rejoins the PCT and saves about a mile, and is the recommended line.

Walk on until you are essentially due EAST of Huckleberry's summit — roughly nine to ten miles in. That bearing is the trigger to leave the trail, not a named junction.

Many parties make this two or three days with a camp at Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake; a fit party has done it car to car in about eleven and a half hours.

About 17.4 km and 4,600 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEAVE THE PCT WHEN THE SUMMIT IS DUE WEST OF YOU — A BEARING, NOT A LANDMARK, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT YOU WANT IN CLOUD. From that point head cross-country WEST up steep heather or talus.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS WHERE THE MELLOW TERRAIN ENDS AND THE GROUND TURNS ROCKY, at about 6,100 ft, marked by a ROCKY BUTTRESS. That change underfoot is the arrival, and it is felt rather than seen.

AND THEN COMES THE ONE DECISION THAT DECIDES WHICH ROUTE YOU CLIMB, WHICH IS THE MOST VALUABLE THING ON THIS PAGE. At the base of the rocks you have two options: LEFT takes you into a steep loose GULLY leading to a notch and the summit block — that is the older Beckey line, and it has turned parties around with rockfall. RIGHT takes you up the RIDGE on class 3+ terrain — that is the East Ridge, the historic first-ascent route, and it is what most parties now climb. If you are in a loose gully, you have gone left.

HOW TO FOLLOW IT ONCE COMMITTED, BECAUSE IT DOES NOT LOOK OBVIOUS FROM BELOW: the route goes up the RIGHT side of the east ridge, essentially linking CLUMPS OF TREES, tree patch to tree patch. Looking up at it, the line is genuinely hard to piece together by eye; once you start, the next move is usually clear. Staying towards the RIGHT is correct at the beginning.

CHECKPOINTS HIGHER UP: about halfway, maybe a little further, leave the ridge proper by heading LEFT on a short traverse to a BLOCKY RAMP, which you climb to a high point just before the summit block. Then descend about 20 ft to the NOTCH at the foot of the block — either straight down, or skiers' right and a class 3 traverse to a ramp leading down to the notch.

THE SUMMIT BLOCK ITSELF: go up the middle to an obvious SLABBY RAMP. From there either a short class 5 crack — one piece, a #1 Camalot at its start, is what the record describes — or follow the ramp climbers' LEFT to exposed class 3/4. Bring a 60 m rope: a 30 m is insufficient for the rappel off the block.

SCALE OF THE THING, SO NOBODY UNDERESTIMATES IT: there is no walk-up on this mountain, the scrambling is stiff class 3 with class 4 moves, and one of the 1915 first-ascent party wrote his will on his shirt cuff over doubts he would survive the descent.
hazards: Stiff class 3 with class 4 moves on an exposed ridge — not a beginners' scramble
A loose block at the notch below the summit block
A crumbly class 2 ledge traverse above a big cliff
Rockfall in the alternative Beckey gully on the left, which has turned parties around
No simple walk-off: a 60 m rope is needed for the rappel off the summit block
A very long day, with parties commonly splitting it over two or three

This row is an IDAHO route on the Selkirk Crest's Chimney Rock, filed on Washington's Chimney Rock, and is already flagged for removal. Note also that the row's own aspect column says E while its name says West Face, which is the same defect seen from the other side.
